children.text:
This is way better than my recollection of SourceTrail when I tried it years ago. SourceTrail was terribly slow and clunky, to the point of being useless for me.

This SrcWranglr compiles and runs without issues on my Linux machine, and I’ve been using it for a few hours.

There are some glitches like the click event on a menu punching through and triggering actions under the menu, for instance the “Reindex” action will also select whatever symbol happens to be under it which is confusing as it makes the central graph display (which looks amazing by the way!) to change giving the impression that the re-index made you lose your position.

Still, it is already very useful and I have added to the handful of tools I use while programming.

I added the shortcut C-R to trigger Reindex. I am preparing the tiny PR although it might be faster for you to just do it by yourself than to adapt my commit.

Ironically, since SrcWranglr does not support Rust I used my own code navigator written in C, which supports more programming languages including Rust although not nearly as many features, to find quickly the places where the shortcuts and menus are defined. I find that you have implemented many things I had hoped to do some day, specifically the value tracing. This is a great tool.

source.text:
SrcWranglr my open-source, Rust-powered C/C++ source-code exploration and security analysis toolkit. I had originally developed this in Python as a prototype for a couple years… That’s until you Rustaceans got in my damn year…

If you ever used SourceTrail or Understand, this is my idea of how it should have been done. It helps visualize complex codebases C/C++ it combines interactive call graphs, cross-references, semantic code search, reachability analysis, and inter-procedural value tracing.

Security-focused features include vulnerability discovery, attack-surface analysis, automated fuzz harness generation, and integration with external static analyzers. My favorite feature is the ability to generate semgrep rules for the specific code base.

Powered by tree-sitter, SrcWranglr can analyze codebases without requiring a successful build or compilation database.

Using this tool and my AAVR (Agentic Augmented Vuln Research) methodology I found several vulnerabilities in projects I won’t name as I just disclose to maintainers, in just a couple of hours.

https://github.com/jdefrancesco/SrcWranglr
